heading: Bethlehem Kudumba Unit review: Nivin, Mamitha power this warm hug of a film
paragraphs: There are films that make you fall in love with love. There are films that make you fall in love with cinema. And then there are films that feel like a warm hug. Director Girish AD’s Bethlehem Kudumba Unit is one such film — full of little moments, innocence, laughter and heart.

Ashley (Mamitha Baiju), her parents and her brother Alan move into a new home opposite Justin’s (Nivin Pauly) in Ernakulam. Justin is the kind of man the entire neighbourhood loves because he is always there for everyone. He runs a catering business and also produces his brother Joel’s (Sangeeth Prathap) short films. Still sad about leaving the home she grew up in, Ashley looks out of her new window and catches sight of Justin seemingly threatening a man. It is hardly the first impression you'd expect of the neighbourhood's favourite guy.

As Ashley slowly warms up to the tight-knit neighbourhood, she develops a liking for Justin, who is 12-13 years older than her. Can they find their happily ever after despite the age gap, her strict parents and the complications that come with it? Girish AD answers that question over two hours and 37 minutes.

Girish AD’s films are realistic, rooted and often cutesy romantic dramas, but what sets them apart are the micro-details he brings to his supporting characters and the worlds they inhabit. Much like Premalu, which helped Mamitha rise to fame, Bethlehem Kudumba Unit has a group of characters who make us believe that there is still hope in the world.

Nivin Pauly’s Justin is an empathetic man who has gone through a loss. He has been in the pits of darkness and perhaps that’s why he is always there for everyone else. He is a good son, friend and brother, and eventually becomes the kind of boyfriend anyone would be lucky to have. Mamitha’s Ashley, meanwhile, is young, brimming with joy and unafraid to express her love, even if it is with a little nudge. Despite the age gap, their romance never feels forced. They simply make it look easy. Ever seen a couple who just seem right for each other? That’s them.

Justin and Ashley aren’t the kind of couple who share mushy dialogues or constantly hold hands. They are companions who talk about everything under the sun, show up for each other and, most importantly, make each other’s lives easier. Their journey isn’t a bed of roses either. They are aware of the age gap, Ashley’s strict parents and her studies. Justin brings his maturity to the relationship, balancing out Ashley’s youthful exuberance.

Nivin Pauly’s vulnerability makes Justin so endearing. He feels like the kind of person everyone needs around them — especially on the days when you cannot be there for yourself. That’s when Justin would swoop in. Mamitha Baiju is on a roll. Last week, she starred in Suriya’s Vishwanath and Sons, which also dealt with an age-gap relationship. Yet the two performances feel remarkably different. Mamitha brings enough personality to Ashley to make her more than just the younger woman in an age-gap romance, and her performance adds to the film’s warmth.

But Bethlehem Kudumba Unit isn’t only interested in whether Justin and Ashley will end up together. The film is also interested in the walls people build around themselves through grief, fear, social expectations and the need to conform. Its supporting characters are often dealing with their own versions of these mental blocks, and Girish AD gently allows them to find their way out rather than turning their problems into grand dramatic conflicts. It is this attention to the little emotional battles that gives the film its warmth.

Roshan Shanavas (of Aavesham fame), Shyam Mohan and a bunch of eccentric supporting characters keep the laughs coming. The comic timing is so impeccable that looking away for even a moment could mean missing a terrific reaction or counter. The humour rarely feels forced because it comes organically from the personalities of these characters.

Cinematographer Ajmal Sabu’s work brings Kerala alive on screen and makes the setting feel like another character in the story. A rom-com like Bethlehem Kudumba Unit also needs music that can carry its emotional and romantic beats, and Vishnu Vijay delivers one of the film’s strongest technical assets, mixing lilting melodies with nostalgic tracks that complement its warmth.

What makes Bethlehem Kudumba Unit work is that it never feels like it is desperately trying to be a feel-good film. It finds joy in ordinary conversations, awkward encounters, eccentric neighbours and the simple act of showing up for someone. The romance between Justin and Ashley is at the centre of it, but the film’s real charm lies in the larger community it creates around them.

This Onam, Nivin Pauly and Mamitha Baiju gift us a fuzzy little film that is all heart. Bethlehem Kudumba Unit may not reinvent the romantic comedy, but it understands something more important: sometimes, a film doesn't need to be revolutionary. It just needs to make you leave the theatre feeling a little lighter.
